POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Fri, 02 Oct 2026 15:14:03 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.9 17 countries join forces to oppose EU budget cuts https://www.politico.eu/article/17-countries-join-forces-to-oppose-eu-budget-cuts/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 02 Oct 2026 14:39:01 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9098864 BRUSSELS — Seventeen EU governments have publicly warned against cuts to agriculture and regional payouts in the next seven-year budget, in a rebuke of Germany’s stance in the negotiations.

The letter — signed on Friday by Italy, Spain and Poland among others — heaps pressure on the Irish rotating presidency of the Council of the EU to leave untouched almost €900 billion of spending in the upcoming draft budget, which is expected to be presented next week.

This sets up tensions with a rival camp of six countries led by Germany, which renewed calls for cuts of several hundred billion euros across the board in a joint letter earlier this week.

“We therefore believe that the overall funding for Cohesion Policy and the CAP must be preserved in the next MFF,” the seventeen countries wrote in the letter to Irish Taoiseach Micheal Martin seen by POLITICO.

The signatories include Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Romanian President Nicușor Dan coordinated the initiative and will host an informal meeting of those countries in the margins of the next European Council on Oct. 15 and 16.

The Multiannual Financial Framework, or MFF, finances everything from farmers’ subsidies to development aid, and is among the toughest negotiations in Brussels. In 2025, the European Commission proposed a budget of nearly €2 trillion for the 2028-2034 period and shifted hundreds of billions from agriculture and regional payouts, known as cohesion policy, to new priorities such as defense and competitiveness.  

The so-called Friends of Cohesion group warned that further reductions to agricultural and cohesion “would only weaken it [budget] and risk undermining public support for the European project.”

Ireland’s negotiating document, or negobox, will set the scene for discussions among the EU’s 27 leaders during the summit in Brussels in October.

EU governments are rushing to secure a final agreement among themselves by the end of the year, before national elections in France, Poland and Italy threaten to derail the negotiations.

One of the most sensitive issues involves introducing new EU-wide taxes, known as own resources, to finance the budget. The Commission proposed five new levies that are estimated to generate €66 billion per year.

The tax package is strongly supported by France, but individual proposals have been opposed by several national governments who fear that they will be disproportionately affected by the levies.

The 17 countries wrote in the letter that new own resources”should be genuine, fair, simple and non-regressive.”

To create more leeway, they also renewed calls to delay repayments of post-Covid debt that is expected to cost €25 billion per year and opposed budget discounts to wealthier countries, known as rebates.

]]> en G7 agrees major release of oil stocks following pressure from the US https://www.politico.eu/article/trump-says-europe-agrees-to-release-massive-amount-of-diesel/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 02 Oct 2026 14:16:12 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9099980 BRUSSELS — The G7 group of rich countries has agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil over the next four months, following intense pressure from the Trump administration for Europe to tap its stockpiles of diesel.

In a joint statement following an emergency meeting on Friday, the G7 leaders said the release of 100 million barrels of oil would “begin immediately” and would start with release of diesel stocks.

The announcement comes after POLITICO reported earlier this week that the U.S. administration had requested European countries to release reserves of diesel into the market to cushion a sharp rise in prices of the fuel, which was becoming a political problem for the Republicans ahead of next month’s midterm elections.

Trump had also threatened  to ban exports of diesel altogether — a major worry for European countries because U.S. diesel accounts for more than half of the continent’s imports of the fuel.

But that threat is now off the table, G7 leaders said Friday. Under the agreement there would be “no restrictions or bans on exports among G7 countries,” the statement read.

French President Emmanuel Macron denied European leaders had been strong-armed into making the concession with the threat of a diesel export, telling press on Friday: “The tone of our discussion was not one of threats; it was constructive.”

He added that Trump had been “very clear” that there would be no export ban.

The leaders’ statement did not specify that the releases would come from European reserves, but U.S. President Donald Trump said in a social media post that European countries had agreed to make a major contribution.

“Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “The process will begin immediately.”

The announcement comes after several rounds of emergency talks between European governments over how to respond to the U.S. pressure, with France proposing a release of 100 million barrels of European oil and diesel earlier Friday.

The G7 includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the U.K. and the U.S.

While G7 countries participated in a release of 400 million barrels of oil earlier this year led by the International Energy Agency, many of the barrels released never made it to market because they were unable to compete with cheaper U.S. crude that has recently flooded the bloc, according to a trader and an EU diplomat. But they were, officially, available, the people said. 

Two other diplomats suggested Friday that the announcement was simply a reaffirmation of that March commitment.

]]> en Šefčovič: Verhandlung mit China noch ohne Ergebnisse https://www.politico.eu/article/sefcovic-verhandlung-mit-china-noch-ohne-ergebnisse/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 02 Oct 2026 14:04:26 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro-free&p=9099692 MILWAUKEE – China und die EU seien in Bezug auf ein mögliches Handelsabkommen „noch lange nicht am Ziel“, sagte EU-Handelskommissar Maroš Šefčovič am Donnerstag (Ortszeit) im Gespräch mit POLITICO. Die Gespräche seien „konstruktiv, aber schwierig“.

„Ich spüre großes politisches Interesse und natürlich sehr hohe Erwartungen seitens der Staats- und Regierungschefs in der gesamten Europäischen Union“, sagte Šefčovič am Rande eines Treffens der G20-Handelsminister in Milwaukee. „Ich weiß, wie politisch ungeduldig die europäische Führung ist.“

Šefčovič reist am 8. Oktober nach Peking für ein, wie er es nannte, „äußerst wichtiges Treffen“ mit dem chinesischen Handelsminister Wang Wentao. Er sei optimistisch, dass die Reise Früchte tragen werde. „Man muss daran glauben, dass man etwas erreichen kann, sonst sollte man besser gar nicht erst hinfahren.“

Über die Ergebnisse der Reise sprechen die EU-Staats- und Regierungschefs am 15. und 16. Oktober bei ihrem EU-Gipfel in Brüssel. Die EU droht damit, den Zugang chinesischer Unternehmen zum Binnenmarkt einzuschränken, sollten die Gespräche scheitern.

Die EU und China verhandeln seit Juni. Die Staats- und Regierungschefs der EU haben erklärt, sie wollten die große Menge chinesischer Importe und das hohe Handelsdefizit mit China, nicht länger hinnehmen.

„Ich glaube, unsere chinesischen Partner haben verstanden, dass dies direkte Auswirkungen auf die Zukunft bedeutender europäischer Unternehmen hat – buchstäblich Tausende von Arbeitsplätzen“, berichtete Šefčovič. „Und auch auf das soziale Gefüge und das Sozialmodell, das in Europa über viele, viele Jahrzehnte hinweg entwickelt wurde.“

Im Mittelpunkt der Gespräche steht das wachsende Handelsdefizit der Union mit China von einer Milliarde Euro pro Tag. Um dieses Defizit zu verringern, müssen die Importe aus China reduziert und/oder die EU-Exporte nach China gesteigert werden.

Šefčovič erklärte, er hoffe, aus Peking Ergebnisse zu drei Hauptthemen mitbringen zu können: plötzliche Exportanstiege Chinas in wichtigen Industriezweigen, Maßnahmen zur Steigerung europäischer Warenexporte nach China, Klarheit hinsichtlich chinesischer Exportbeschränkungen für Rohstoffe, insbesondere für Seltene Erden.

In Milwaukee traf sich Šefčovič mit dem chinesischen Vizeminister Li Chenggang. Der slowakische Kommissar erklärte, China habe Verständnis für die Bedenken Europas: „Alle von uns angesprochenen Themen liegen auf dem Tisch. Ich sage nicht, dass wir Zusicherungen haben, dass wir sie lösen werden, aber sie liegen auf dem Tisch.“

In der Vergangenheit hätten sich einige dieser Themen nur schwer auf die Tagesordnung setzen lassen. Dass dies nun möglich ist, „spiegelt das Bewusstsein dafür wider, wie wichtig dies politisch für uns beide ist“, sagte der Kommissar.

Die Gespräche der EU mit China wurden bisher in vier Arbeitsbereiche unterteilt: Handels- und Investitionsgleichgewicht, Exportkontrollen, geistiges Eigentum und die Reform der Welthandelsorganisation WTO.

Eine mit den Verhandlungen vertraute Person erklärte, die Kommission strebe eine Einigung mit China an, die eine Mischung aus bilateralen Abkommen für bestimmte Produktgruppen und einseitigen Beschränkungen für andere Kategorien vorsehe.

]]> de Feijóo: In Ceuta, it’s up to Europe to clean up the Spanish government’s mess https://www.politico.eu/article/in-ceuta-its-up-to-europe-to-clean-up-the-spanish-governments-mess/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 02 Oct 2026 10:51:49 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9099095 Alberto Núñez Feijóo is Spain’s leader of the opposition and the president of the People’s Party.

On July 30, at least 80,000 people crossed into Ceuta from Morocco, the largest violation of territorial integrity we have experienced in recent decades. That challenge tested the resilience of Spain’s southern border and, therefore, of Europe’s southern border. It continues 50 days later. With no clear prospect of when it might be resolved. It is therefore time to ask ourselves whether our response matches the scale of what is at stake.

A border is not just a line on a map. It is the expression of a political community that decides which values to protect and which responsibilities to share. When a European border is breached, Europe as a whole becomes weaker. When a border is not properly defended, Europe as a whole is left unprotected. That is what is happening.

The response of the current Spanish government, incapable of acknowledging the true nature of the problem and implementing the correct solution, obliges me to reiterate, first and foremost, the obvious, as the President of Ceuta did last week during his visit to Brussels. We are not witnessing a conventional migration crisis, but rather the consequences of an invasion originating from Morocco, which must therefore be held responsible for having condoned or instigated it.

Normality has disappeared from Ceuta for more than six weeks, and the scenes of chaos, overcrowding and insecurity should both shame us and compel us to act. To think that the prolongation of this situation will have no consequences is a mistake we cannot afford to make: it affects our sovereignty, our collective capacity to defend the rule of law, the safety of our citizens, and the credibility of the European project in ensuring its own stability.

Undoubtedly, the national authorities are the first to bear the responsibility for resolving this crisis, in accordance with a non-negotiable principle shared by all EU member states under the Pact on Migration and Asylum: those who have entered irregularly must be returned. All of them. The Spanish government’s obligation is not to find accommodation for them, but to expedite their departure.

That said, given the time that has elapsed and the escalation of violent incidents in Ceuta, Europe as a whole must recognize the failure of the Spanish government and exert the necessary pressure to prevent this crisis from becoming entrenched, spreading, or happening again. Just as Europe has responded when faced with other hybrid threats — on energy, trade or disinformation — the attack on our southern border now demands the same determination.

Firstly, the European Union must ensure that Spain implements, with due rigor and efficiency, all the European instruments available to facilitate returns. Secondly, it must clarify why the Kingdom of Morocco itself has reiterated in an official statement its willingness to take back all those who entered on July 30, while Spanish ministers maintain that no such cooperation exists.

Thirdly, it must make full use of all its diplomatic resources to ensure that the relationship with Morocco, a strategic partner for Spain and for the rest of Europe, continues to develop on the basis of transparency and mutual respect. While I advocate the need to establish a loyal and stable relationship with our neighboring country, I believe it is in the interests of the entire European Union to ensure that this relationship is not undermined by the exploitation of migration flows or by the questioning of the Spanish identity of Ceuta and Melilla, territories that are just as European as Berlin, Paris or Brussels.

Finally, I would like to stress that humanity cannot be used as an excuse for inaction in response to what has happened. It is true that the attack on Ceuta did not involve soldiers, that many of those who crossed Europe’s southern border were themselves victims and that, in fact, more than a hundred people died. But contrary to what some cynically claim, it is precisely humanity that compels us to discourage people from risking their lives at sea: this must cease to be a valid means of reaching Europe.

As many know, I aspire to become the next prime minister of Spain. Consequently, it is my duty to seek the support of the European Union and all of its member states for my country at this crucial moment. The first duty of a leader is to guarantee the safety of citizens, defend national sovereignty and uphold the credibility of institutions. But this also reflects a commitment to a certain way of understanding Europe, one that I personally share with all our allies: the responsibility to safeguard its territorial integrity and its values is a shared one. Now it is our turn to defend Ceuta, Spain and Europe.

]]> en Tories warn Burnham’s EU ‘pandering’ will shred post-Brexit trade deals https://www.politico.eu/article/tories-andy-burnham-eu-pandering-threatens-post-brexit-trade-deals/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 02 Oct 2026 10:28:42 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9095324 LONDON — The architects of Britain’s first post-Brexit trade deals have warned that the country’s independent trade policy is under threat after Andy Burnham pledged a major review of its relationship with the EU. 

Their intervention marks the latest salvo in a political fightback against Burnham’s EU policy as the Conservative Party conference gets underway in Birmingham this weekend.

Burnham this week vowed to discuss a revamped relationship with Europe, including rejoining the EU’s customs union, moving closer the bloc’s single market — or even pushing to outright rejoin the bloc. It marks a fundamental shift from a Labour Party that has previously ruled out all three.

Customs union membership — a popular option among some members of Burnham’s Cabinet — would ease trade between the U.K. and its largest trading partner, but require Britain to sacrifice the trade deals it has struck since leaving the bloc six years ago.

Greg Hands, who served as trade minister four times between 2016 to 2024 under Conservative governments, said that all options presented “grave consequences for Britain’s independent trade policy.”

“Depending exactly on what is agreed, it is likely to invalidate or make very difficult most — if not all — of those existing trade agreements, or many of those existing trade agreements,” he said. 

Since Brexit, the U.K. has negotiated free trade deals with nations including Australia, New Zealand, Japan and — more recently — the Asia Pacific trading bloc CPTPP, India, the Gulf states, as well as upgraded deals with South Korea and Switzerland.

Although the U.K. could technically copy-and paste EU versions of trade deals, Hands warned that the terms might not be so favorable, highlighting that the U.K.-Japan deal he had helped to negotiate “has got much more liberal rules on data” than the EU equivalent.

As a non-EU member, the U.K. would also surrender its ability to negotiate the terms of any new trade deals, Hands argued. “Why would the EU prioritize the U.K., which is not a paying member of the EU, over paying full members of the EU when it does trade agreements?”

But the issue goes further than free trade agreements, he said, pointing out that entering a customs union with the EU would affect the U.K.’s global tariff — the independent system of taxes and duty rates applied to goods imported from other countries. This would be a “huge diminution of the U.K.’s influence in the world to align or take the EU’s customs tariff,” Hands added.

Moreover, by signing up to a customs union, the U.K. would also lose its ability to erect its own trade defenses and be forced to implement EU measures like tariffs on steel and electric vehicles, Hands warned.

He also cautioned that closer alignment could complicate relations with the U.S., which has been critical of U.K. ambitions for closer alignment with the EU. “The U.S. is our single largest bilateral trading partner and I don’t think it would be in the U.K.’s interest to mess up that relationship.”

End of CPTPP membership

Liam Fox, a self-proclaimed “staunch euroskeptic” who served as trade secretary in the immediate aftermath of the referendum, between 2016 and 2019, said rejoining the EU or customs union would “mean an end to Britain’s independent trade policy and any strategy influence we have from membership of organizations such as [the Asia-Pacific trade bloc] CPTPP.” 

“This vague language from Andy Burnham is all about keeping the Labour left quiet whatever the consequences,” Fox added. “Rejoining the EU would mean being part of Schengen with free movement of people and adoption of the Euro. If that is what Andy Burnham wants, let him make the case for it, stop his mealy-mouthed pandering to his own party and start acting like a real prime minister.”

A third former Tory trade minister — granted anonymity to speak frankly — told MTUK the risks to Britain’s new trade deals was “real” and would “undermine new relationships with some of the fastest growing middle-class economies in the world.”

“As the mature EU markets continue to be a smaller part of U.K. export opportunities, the prime minister should be focusing on supporting U.K. businesses to win export contracts where huge new markets exist,” the former minister argued.

]]> en Diesel : sous la pression des Etats-Unis, l’exécutif envisage de libérer une part importante de ses réserves https://www.politico.eu/article/diesel-sous-la-pression-des-etats-unis-lexecutif-envisage-de-liberer-une-part-importante-de-ses-reserves/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 02 Oct 2026 10:01:09 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9098762 BRUXELLES — Lors de discussions d’urgence vendredi, le gouvernement français a évoqué la possibilité de libérer une partie des stocks stratégiques de pétrole et de gazole, après que l’administration Trump a fait pression sur les pays européens pour qu’ils mettent leurs réserves sur le marché, a appris POLITICO de deux personnes au fait des échanges.

La proposition faite par le gouvernement français lors d’une réunion de hauts responsables européens ce vendredi est que les pays de l’UE libèrent 50 millions de barils de pétrole brut et 50 millions de barils de gazole. Une idée qui fait encore l’objet d’une évaluation technique, a précisé l’un des interlocuteurs.

Cette décision intervient après que le secrétaire américain à l’Energie, Chris Wright, a demandé aux pays européens de libérer 120 millions de barils de leurs stocks sur une période de trois mois afin de lutter contre la hausse des prix du diesel, sous peine de se voir imposer des restrictions à l’importation de diesel américain. Selon ces sources, la proposition de compromis faite vendredi par la France faisait suite à une nouvelle demande adressée par les Etats-Unis au président français Emmanuel Macron, lui demandant de libérer 100 millions de barils de diesel.

L’Elysée a indiqué ce matin qu’Emmanuel Macron avait échangé pendant la nuit avec Donald Trump “pour évoquer la situation énergétique mondiale”, et notamment pour “garantir la disponibilité des produits raffinés au niveau mondial”. La France, qui assure la présidence tournante du G7 “entend réunir dans les meilleurs délais une visioconférence des dirigeants du G7 pour assurer la coordination des mesures à prendre afin de contribuer à desserrer l’étau des prix”.

Lors de l’échange ce vendredi matin, le gouvernement allemand s’est montré réticent à débloquer le moindre baril, selon ces sources. “L’Allemagne et d’autres pays ne veulent pas servir de pions ; ils souhaitent ne libérer leurs stocks que pour de véritables raisons de sécurité d’approvisionnement”, a déclaré l’une d’entre elles à POLITICO, s’exprimant sous couvert d’anonymat afin de pouvoir s’exprimer en toute franchise. L’Allemagne et la France disposent des plus importantes réserves de pétrole et de produits pétroliers en Europe, selon les statistiques officielles de l’UE.

“La France tient à participer et à répondre à cette demande […] Il est clair que l’UE agira, dans la mesure où ses membres parviendront à s’entendre”, a déclaré une deuxième source. Elle a ajouté qu’il était difficile de savoir si cette libération serait coordonnée conjointement par l’UE ou menée sur une base bilatérale, compte tenu de l’approche “désordonnée” des Etats-Unis, qui ont adressé des demandes différentes à différents pays. “C’est une méthode typiquement américaine : ils ne passent pas par les voies officielles habituelles.”

Le cabinet du ministre Roland Lescure, présent à la réunion vendredi matin, a balayé auprès de POLITICO des “rumeurs” et ne souhaite pas commenter davantage.

Les Etats-Unis montrent une frustration croissante à l’égard des pays de l’UE qui n’ont pas tenu leurs engagements de contribuer à la mise sur le marché de 400 millions de barils, opération coordonnée en début d’année par l’Agence internationale de l’énergie à la suite du déclenchement de la guerre en Iran et de la fermeture du détroit d’Ormuz.

Lors de la réunion qui s’est tenue vendredi à Bruxelles, certains représentants européens ont également critiqué la France et l’Allemagne pour ne pas avoir mis sur le marché des réserves pétrolières substantielles, selon l’une des personnes présentes.

POLITICO a rapporté jeudi que les principaux pays de l’UE et le Royaume-Uni souhaitaient répondre aux pressions américaines d’une voix « ferme », tout en cherchant à apaiser les tensions.

There initially appeared to be enough parliamentary support to pass at least one decree. But late on Thursday, the Catalan separatist Junts party, which defends landlords’ rights, announced it would oppose both measures, ensuring their defeat.

Sánchez responded defiantly to Junts’ move, saying on X he would not withdraw the decrees and casting the parliamentary vote as a breaking point: “The hour of truth has arrived,” he wrote, adding that lawmakers were obliged to cast “votes that will define them for generations to come.”

With housing consistently ranking among Spaniards’ top concerns, Sánchez now looks set to try to capitalize on popular discontent by casting the opposition as an obstacle to addressing the crisis.

The center-right People’s Party leads in electoral polls, with 34% support. Its potential partner, the far-right Vox party, is polling at 18%. Both oppose measures that challenge landlords’ property rights and instead favor deregulation and incentives for private owners.

At the request of Sánchez’s Socialist Party and far-left Sumar, which make up Spain’s coalition government, Friday’s vote was conducted by a show of hands, forcing lawmakers to publicly reveal their positions on the government’s housing measures.

Friday’s parliamentary vote came amid nationwide demonstrations over the housing crisis, with protest encampments in major Spanish cities. As the session began, protesters in Madrid marched toward the parliament, where they were met by more than 1,000 national police officers protecting the building.

The Spanish Tenants’ Union, which is leading the protests, is calling for a general strike and vowing to continue occupying the capital’s central Puerta del Sol square until their demands are met.

Spain’s national government has so far declined a request from Madrid’s local and regional governments to clear the square. Center-right regional President Isabel Díaz Ayuso has filed suit in court demanding Sánchez’s government be ordered to clear the protest in Madrid; a ruling is expected this afternoon.

]]> en France floats major oil and diesel reserve release in response to US pressure https://www.politico.eu/article/france-floats-major-release-of-oil-and-diesel-reserves-in-response-to-us-pressure/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 02 Oct 2026 09:23:54 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9098540 BRUSSELS — French officials proposed a large release of strategic oil and diesel reserves during emergency talks Friday after Washington urged European capitals to tap stockpiles or face a potentially crippling ban on fuel exports, according to two officials briefed on the meeting.

Under a proposal made during a gathering of senior European energy officials Friday, Paris suggested that EU countries release 50 million barrels of crude oil and 50 million barrels of diesel, according to the officials. The idea is still undergoing technical assessment, said one of the officials.

It comes after U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright asked European countries to release 120 million barrels from stockpiles over a three-month period to combat rising diesel prices or else face export restrictions. According to the officials, France’s compromise offer Friday was in response to a fresh request by the U.S. to French President Emmanuel Macron to release 100 million barrels of fuel, all of which should be diesel.

Berlin, on the other hand, was reluctant to release any barrels, according to the officials. “Germany and others don’t want to be used; they wish to release stocks only for real security of supply reasons,” one of them told POLITICO, speaking on condition of anonymity to speak candidly, as with others in this piece. Germany and France have the largest reserves of oil and petroleum products in Europe, according to official EU statistics.

“France is keen to participate and meet the request … it’s clear the EU will do something, to the extent they can agree on something,” said the second person. They added that it was unclear whether the release would be jointly coordinated by the EU or done on a bilateral basis, given the “messy” approach by the U.S., which has sent different requests to different countries. “It’s a typical US request — they don’t go through the official normal channels.”

A spokesperson for French Economy Minister Roland Lescure dismissed the proposal as “rumors” and declined to comment further. In a statement, the Elysée palace said Emmanuel Macron will convene a meeting of G7 leaders “as soon as possible to coordinate the measures needed to help ease the pressure on prices and ensure the supply of crude oil and refined products among G7 countries and globally.”

Macron had a phone call with U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday night to “discuss the global energy situation” and “ensure the global availability of refined products,” the Elysée said.

European Commission spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen said on Friday a ban on diesel exports “would undermine our trust in the United States as a reliable partner,” adding: “We are ready for collective action in the context of the IEA. It is their role to organize possible stock release.”

U.K. officials are expecting a G7 meeting to be convened as soon as Friday, but immediate outcomes are unlikely, according to a person familiar with the matter, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive fuel supply issues. Any European release of reserves would be IEA-led, the person said.

The U.S. is increasingly frustrated at EU countries that have failed to deliver on commitments to contribute to the 400 million barrel release coordinated earlier this year by the International Energy Agency following the outbreak of the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. In the high-level Energy Union Taskforce meeting Friday, some EU countries also rounded on France and Germany for their failure to release substantial oil reserves into the market, according to one of the officials.

POLITICO reported Thursday that leading EU countries and the U.K. wanted to respond to the U.S. pressure with an “assertive” voice while seeking to de-escalate.

Nicolas Camut and Charlie Cooper contributed reporting.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Fri, 02 Oct 2026 15:14:05 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.2 Brunner takes victory lap on irregular arrivals as Syrian asylum claims collapse for reasons beyond EU policy https://euobserver.com/240841/brunner-takes-victory-lap-on-irregular-arrivals-as-syrian-asylum-claims-collapse-for-reasons-beyond-eu-policy/ Fri, 02 Oct 2026 15:14:05 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240841 Syria's regime collapsed in December 2024, over 22 months ago. The country was the largest source of irregular arrivals in 2023. Today, the EU disingenuously attributes its migration policies for the drop of arrivals.]]> The sharp drop in irregular migrant arrivals is evidence that the EU’s policy reforms are working, EU migration commissioner, Magnus Brunner, said on Thursday (1 October).

But Syria is also no longer the single biggest source of asylum claims after the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime 22 months ago, a factor that appears to have been conveniently ignored.

On Thursday, he told reporters after a meeting of EU interior ministers in Luxembourg that irregular arrivals have dropped 55 percent in the past two years.

“So that’s a record low in the asylum applications,” said the former Austrian finance minister, adding that Austria and Sweden have recorded equally low asylum numbers and that Germany is deporting more people than are asking for protection.

“The basis for all of that, and the foundation for all of that, is the pact, the pact on migration and asylum,” he said, in comments that were echoed by Ireland’s migration minister, Jim O’Callaghan.

The pact, spanning a mix of complex regulations, was launched in June. Despite having two years to prepare for the launch, its implementation remains patchy.

]]> French far-right leader Bardella denies writing antisemitic messages https://euobserver.com/240887/french-far-right-leader-bardella-denies-writing-antisemitic-messages/ Fri, 02 Oct 2026 15:13:01 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240887 Jordan Bardella, a leader of the French far-right National Rally, has denied writing antisemitic messages in 2013.]]> Jordan Bardella, a leader of the French far-right National Rally, has denied writing antisemitic messages in 2013, as the race ahead of next May’s presidential elections continues to heat up.

An investigation by the left-leaning outlet Mediapart said on Thursday (1 October) that it could authenticate antisemitic messages from 2013 and attribute them to Bardella.

In the messages, Bardella, an MEP and chair of the far-right Patriots for Europe group, said “all the banks are owned by Jews” and that Israel aims to create a new world order. Earlier media reports also found his secret Twitter account publishing racist content, such as mocking a young Black man who had suffered police violence.

He denied having written the messages, calling the evidence “crude montages” and “obscure screenshots that can easily be manipulated,”  he wrote on social media, adding he would sue Mediapart for defamation.

“Either Mediapart is running this operation itself, or it is being manipulated by interested parties,” he has said.

]]> Magyar waives his own immunity, as Hungary targets billions in alleged fraud and two former Orbán ministers in custody (Day 143 of the Tisza government) https://euobserver.com/240728/magyar-waives-his-own-immunity-as-hungary-targets-billions-in-alleged-fraud-and-two-former-orban-ministers-in-custody-day-143-of-the-tisza-government/ Fri, 02 Oct 2026 11:38:26 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240728 PM Peter Magyar waives his own immunity as Hungary's "Operation Purgatory" saw authorities detain two former Orbán ministers over alleged multibillion-forint corruption. The new asset recovery office took over four major cases, including Orbán's brother's visa business, while Hungary may soon join the European Public Prosecutor's Office.]]> More than a year ago, we launched our Hungary Briefing, a weekly round-up of the election campaign. Since the historic vote in April to remove Viktor Orbán, the series has followed the new Tisza government and its first moves in office. This week’s topics:

  • Two ministers from Orbán’s government have been held in custody.
  • Former prime minister Orbán may have ordered the detention of Ukrainian cash couriers.
  • The newly established National Asset Recovery and Protection Office has begun work.
  • The European Public Prosecutor’s Office could also help recover stolen funds.

It has been an eventful few days in Hungarian public life. Efforts to hold former officials accountable are gathering pace: two former ministers have been remanded in custody over suspected breaches of fiduciary duty involving billions of forints and the acceptance of bribes.

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) immediately took over four cases and began investigating them, including the visa business linked to Orbán’s brother. Meanwhile, a chief prosecutor who resigned from his post claimed in an open letter that Orbán himself had ordered the detention of Ukrainian cash couriers.

Two ministers from Orbán’s government have been held in custody

“The landing is beginning as part of ‘Operation Purgatory’,” prime minister Péter Magyar announced on Monday (28 September) morning. Later that morning, Hungary’s parliament lifted the immunity of Miklós Seszták, an MP and former development minister from the Christian Democratic People’s Party (KDNP); Balázs Hankó, an MP and former culture and innovation minister from Fidesz; and prime minister Magyar.

Prosecutors requested that Hankó’s immunity be lifted on suspicion of breach of fiduciary duty: he is suspected of causing losses of 17 billion forints (€46.5m) to the state budget. Authorities are investigating Seszták on suspicion of accepting bribes and other offences. The former minister and the then chief executive of Hungarian National Asset Management are suspected of receiving approximately 12.6 billion forints (€34.2m), in bribes through an intermediary between 2015 and 2018.

Magyar himself requested the lifting of his own immunity after the deputy prosecutor general asked the speaker of parliament to initiate the procedure over an incident in June 2024. According to the Office of the Prosecutor General, Magyar deliberately dropped the phone of a man filming him into the Danube, an act it classifies legally as theft.

After the vote on his immunity, Seszták went to the Central Investigating Chief Prosecutor’s Office, where he was taken into custody. He said he had committed no crime and wished to give a statement. On Wednesday, a court ordered the former minister’s remand in custody.

Hankó initially waited in the Fidesz parliamentary group’s office for police to take him away. Under the rules, however, he should have presented himself at the Central Investigating Chief Prosecutor’s Office.

Under the Act on the National Assembly, police may enter the parliament building and take action there only with the speaker’s specific permission, while the Parliamentary Guard may neither forcibly bring him before the authorities nor take coercive measures against him. Parliament speaker Ágnes Forsthoffer therefore firmly called on Hankó to leave the building and cooperate with the investigating authorities.

Hankó subsequently held a press conference with his wife and children present, claiming that he was the target of a politically-fabricated case and declaring his innocence. He finally accepted the summons at 7.20 pm and left parliament, setting off to give a statement amid carefully-staged scenes. Orbán’s social media page live-streamed the entire episode (while the Fidesz leader was in Belfast cheering on Hungary’s national football team).

In a statement, prosecutors said that Hankó and his associates had used National Cultural Fund resources for purposes other than those prescribed by law on 1,079 occasions between 3 September 2025 and 30 March 2026.

]]> From the Netherlands to Sierra Leone: EU aid, a president’s daughter and Europe’s most‑wanted cocaine boss https://euobserver.com/240782/from-the-netherlands-to-sierra-leone-eu-aid-a-presidents-daughter-and-europes-mostwanted-cocaine-boss/ Fri, 02 Oct 2026 11:13:13 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240782 Jos Leijdekkers was sentenced in the Netherlands in absentia to 24 years in prison for smuggling seven tonnes of cocaine, robbery, and ordering a killing. But he is also the partner of Agnes Bio, the president of Sierra Leone's daughter.]]> The EU has played down claims by the Dutch government that the bloc’s decision to suspend aid support for Sierra Leone was because the west African country refused to extradite one of the world’s most-wanted drug traffickers to face trial in the Netherlands. 

Speaking on Thursday, (1 October) after a meeting of EU justice ministers in Luxembourg, migration commissioner Magnus Brunner told reporters that the decision to suspend support was made for “technical reasons” — but without giving more detail.  

Sierra Leone was allocated €352m in EU funding between 2021 and 2027, under the bloc’s seven-year budget framework. The country was set to receive €18m from the EU this year. 

But Dutch justice minister David Van Weel insists that the suspension of funds is the result of months of pressure from the Dutch government to persuade president Julius Maada Bio’s government to hand over convicted Dutch drug trafficker Jos Leijdekkers.

]]> Ceuta has become a laboratory for the degradation and dehumanisation of migrants https://euobserver.com/240761/ceuta-has-become-a-laboratory-for-the-degradation-and-dehumanisation-of-migrants/ Fri, 02 Oct 2026 10:43:01 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240761 We went to Ceuta to see how Europe treats people who arrive at its borders. We came back asking how Europe can still call itself a continent governed by law. What we saw there was the often abstract failure of migration policy made brutally concrete: the daily humiliation of human beings.]]> We went to Ceuta to see how Europe treats people who arrive at its borders. We came back asking how Europe can still call itself a continent governed by law.

What we saw there was the often abstract failure of migration policy made brutally concrete: the daily humiliation of human beings — people sleeping under plastic sheets, children left without protection, food distributed under military guard, allegations of beatings and torture, and migrants treated as a threat rather than as people with rights.

These are scenes we never expected to encounter in Europe in 2026. Yet we saw them ourselves. And now that we have seen them, we cannot pretend we did not.

Morally unthinkable and unacceptable

In Ceuta, the boundaries of what is morally unthinkable and unacceptable have been crossed.

Migrants and those who help them are living in a kind of state of exception, where European law has been suspended and prolonged arbitrary police and military rule prevails.

Ceuta is a city abandoned by Spain, Europe and the law, where people are segregated according to their origin in circumstances that recall apartheid regimes. It has become a laboratory for the degradation and dehumanisation of migrants.

The future of Europe is being decided there.

Read more

[Interview] Ceuta crisis shows how EU border outsourcing puts children at risk, says German lawyer

We visited locations where thousands of people are living in undignified conditions, under makeshift shelters, plastic tarpaulins or in the open, assisted by local residents and NGOs such as No Name Kitchen.

They described constant harassment, insults, threats, public targeting through leaked photographs, and the detention of five members accused of disobeying authorities after recording a police operation involving migrants.

First, the far-right Spanish party Vox turned desperate people into prey to be “hunted down one by one”. Eventually, those trying to feed or assist them also became targets. When a group is sufficiently dehumanised, those who try to help them can be dehumanised too.

At Trampolín beach, we saw how the Red Cross distributes, once a day, a single bag of cold food: bread, water, tuna, juice and biscuits, under the watch of National Police vans.

Migrants from other areas can walk for hours to reach it. One day, we witnessed military forces preventing the Red Cross from distributing the same ration to around 1,000 people.

Whether someone eats can depend on military personnel, who can remove people from the queue or deny them food. The food distribution also coincides with Red Cross medical assistance, forcing some people to choose between eating and having their wounds treated.

Children alone on the streets

We spoke with children living on the streets, alone, hungry and cold, without adequate protection. We were told that National Police officers sometimes refuse to identify children who approach them for help, preventing them from entering the protection system.

This is compounded by the refusal of autonomous communities governed by Spain’s centre-right People’s Party and Vox to take them in, and by the Ceuta government’s refusal to appoint legal representatives.

We also heard allegations concerning Ceuta University Hospital. Migrants can face separate treatment at the emergency department and, according to migrants and NGOs, military personnel guarding the entrance prevent them from waiting inside, including minors.

We heard the account of a child with a fractured leg who, after being treated by Médicos Mundi, was allegedly told at the hospital to “go back to your country and see a specialist” and given ibuprofen. In another case, someone was allegedly told: “We are not going to treat you because you have invaded us.”

We also received accounts of torture and cruel, degrading and inhuman treatment by regular military forces and the Legion. Migrants and NGOs described nighttime patrols involving harassment, humiliation, theft, destruction of mobile phones and beatings after people had been restrained with cable ties.

Some were allegedly forced to shave their heads or kneel to kiss a Christian cross. We are particularly concerned by allegations involving women and girls subjected to sexual humiliation.

This is extremely serious. The state is going on the hunt, while those who should protect these people are violating their rights. First came photographs, then video footage published by elDiario.es.

These were not images from the West Bank. They were from Ceuta. First there were allegations. Now there are images. Defence minister Margarita Robles must give explanations.

These soldiers should no longer be patrolling Ceuta’s streets. Article 51 of Spain’s Organic Law on the Disciplinary Regime of the Armed Forces allows for their provisional removal from duty. We have asked the minister to act immediately.

We also documented allegations of daily racist, xenophobic and Islamophobic harassment. Migrants and racialised people are reportedly prevented from entering the city centre, shops and supermarkets by military personnel who decide, based on skin colour or clothing, who can pass.

Racial profiling also affects Ceutíes of Moroccan origin or perceived as such. Some of us were even asked to leave a city-centre restaurant because we were accompanied by a human rights activist and a racialised person.

Read more

Ceuta’s migration crisis is becoming a gift to Spain’s (and Europe’s) far-right

Our political assessment is clear: what is happening in Ceuta should not happen. We cannot become accustomed to systematic violations of human rights against migrants and those who assist them.

Responsibility lies with perpetrators, but also with political leaders, including those in Vox and the PP, far-right influencers spreading hate speech, and media outlets amplifying it by calling human beings “invaders”. When a child becomes an “invader”, his innocence can disappear in the eyes of those who hear that language, opening the door to dehumanisation.

The solution is to enforce the law, ensure accountability and transfer migrants to mainland Spain, where there are sufficient places to accommodate them in dignified conditions while their administrative status is resolved.

But the right does not want solutions.

They want migrants sleeping on beaches and streets in increasingly degrading conditions. They want Ceuta to remain a giant television set, a powder keg from which migrants can be portrayed as an “invasion”, insecurity and chaos used to fuel hatred and racist violence.

Their electoral campaign has begun in Ceuta. The socialist part of the government, afraid of being portrayed by the right as weak, refuses to transfer migrants to the mainland and keeps them trapped there. Those who want to set Ceuta on fire are pouring the petrol; those who could put out the fire are letting them do it.

]]> Why young men are drawn to the far right and young women to the far left https://euobserver.com/240322/why-young-men-are-drawn-to-the-far-right-and-young-women-to-the-far-left/ Fri, 02 Oct 2026 08:58:07 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240322 Gender now splits the youngest voters more than class or education. Many young men feel sidelined by a shifting balance and vote far-right while young women vote far-left.]]> First published in Respekt.

In Germany’s recent state elections, voters as young as 16 could cast ballots. The results confirmed a global trend of political division between young women and men.

“On 1 January, we both deleted Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat. And whichever of us would be the first to start watching Reels again or download Instagram would have to eat a slice of rotten cheese,” Greta and Lena told Germany’s Deutschlandfunk radio station.

The 16-year-old girls live in a village in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and chose to delete social media because they had been spending far too much time on it. They often scrolled on TikTok or Instagram late into the night, affecting their performance at school. This summer, however, both reinstalled TikTok for a month. This time without the punishment of a slice of rotten cheese.

They did so for an experiment with journalists from Deutschlandfunk. The journalists wanted to find out what political content the girls would consume through TikTok, the popular Chinese social network, during the peak of the election campaign. Mecklenburg-Vorpommern went to the polls on the third weekend of September. And, as is well known, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) swept the state, just as it had two weeks prior in Saxony-Anhalt.

Read more

Merz ‘fighting for political survival’ as AfD takes another state and The Left wins Berlin

Greta and Lena, however, were in a markedly different position from their peers in Saxony-Anhalt. For the first time, the north-eastern federal state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern had allowed 16- and 17-year-olds to vote in state elections. Since young people consume much of their news on social media, Greta and Lena immersed themselves in TikTok, one of the networks now most popular among young Europeans.

For the first few minutes, the girls watched a range of non-political videos — recipes, tomato growing and “silly” AI videos. Then, at around the third minute of scrolling, the first political content appeared. First came a video about Erich Honecker, the former East German communist politician. “Why am I seeing so much stuff about the GDR here?” Greta wondered. As she continued scrolling, she came across AfD co-leader Alice Weidel herself.

It was the first moment when the girls began to notice how quickly their initially apolitical feed was changing. “I feel as if it is constantly just AfD,” Greta said later. She added that she had not searched for any such content in advance. Over the following month, the girls kept a diary of their feed and observed how, after political videos, more and more similar content began appearing — not only from the parties themselves, but also from a range of accounts that picked up and further spread their messages.

The experiment confirmed what has been known for some time: TikTok and other networks alongside it can quickly form the political world a young person sees and the views they come to adopt. At the same time, algorithms are accelerating a trend of a political divide between young women and men, which was also reflected in the results of the state elections mentioned above in Germany.

]]> Europe’s Affordable Housing Act must look beyond short-term rentals https://euobserver.com/240606/europes-affordable-housing-act-must-look-beyond-short-term-rentals/ Fri, 02 Oct 2026 08:35:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240606 As Brussels pins its housing fix on curbing Airbnb-style rentals, campaigners warn lawmakers are ducking a far bigger fight over Europe’s millions of empty homes and the people still sleeping rough.]]> The appointment of a dedicated Commissioner for Energy and Housing, the launch of the European Affordable Housing Plan, and growing political attention to Europe’s housing crisis raised expectations of a comprehensive policy response.

The next legislative step was therefore expected to address one of the Union’s most pressing social challenges. The proposed Affordable Housing Act is an important step in that direction. Yet its binding Regulation focuses primarily on one specific aspect of the problem: restrictions on non-primary housing use, particularly short-term rentals, in areas under housing stress.

While addressing short-term rentals is a welcome intention, it cannot on its own provide a comprehensive response to Europe’s housing crisis. 

The pressure that holiday homes and short-term rental platforms are putting on housing markets, particularly in popular tourist destinations, has been rising, and giving local authorities better tools to respond is important. However, questions have already been raised about whether the proposed framework will give cities sufficient room to act effectively.

For instance, the proposed approach to defining “areas under housing stress” risks being too narrow. Housing stress cannot be understood through property prices, income levels and short-term projections alone. Energy poverty, combined housing and energy costs, overcrowding, vacancy rates and the condition of existing housing stock all influence whether households can access decent and affordable homes. A broader understanding of housing stress would better reflect the reality facing communities across Europe.

Yet the broader picture reveals an important limitation: many of the structural drivers of housing unaffordability remain outside the scope of the binding Regulation. In particular, it gives limited attention to one of Europe’s most significant untapped housing resources: the buildings and homes that already exist.

Renovation, adaptive re-use and the mobilisation of vacant and underused buildings feature in the European Affordable Housing Plan and the Recommendation accompanying the Act. But if Europe is serious about increasing affordable housing stock, these approaches should play a stronger role in the framework itself.

Across the EU, more than 47 million dwellings are estimated to be unoccupied. This does not mean that every empty home can or should be brought back into use. But it illustrates the scale of an existing resource that cannot be ignored. Bringing even a fraction of suitable vacant and underused stock back into use could create much-needed homes while reducing pressure for new construction and making better use of existing buildings and infrastructure.

Europe cannot reuse buildings it cannot see. Yet many public authorities still lack reliable information about which homes and buildings are vacant, why they are empty, what condition they are in and what potential they have for affordable housing.

The EU does not need to start from scratch. The Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD) and National Building Renovation Plans already provide a natural policy framework for understanding and planning the future of Europe’s building stock. Vacancy identification, mapping and monitoring should become part of the binding architecture of the Affordable Housing Act, ensuring that public authorities are, at a minimum, equipped to identify vacant and underused homes and assess their potential for conversion into decent and affordable homes.

Identifying vacant buildings, however, is only the first step. The accompanying Recommendation could go further by providing guidance on how to mobilise vacant properties, support the conversion of different building types and develop viable financing models.

EU financing should also better support the mobilisation and re-use of existing buildings. The next EU budget should continue to support affordable housing investment and recognise that renovation and re-use projects simultaneously deliver social, climate and energy benefits.

Ultimately, however, success cannot be measured only in buildings renovated or investment mobilised. It must be measured in whether people can access decent homes they can afford.

According to the Commission’s EU Anti-Poverty Strategy, one in five Europeans – nearly 93 million people – are at risk of poverty or social exclusion, while approximately 1 million people experience homelessness. Affordable housing policy must therefore place particular emphasis on those least well served by the housing market, including lower-income households and people experiencing or at risk of housing exclusion.

The Affordable Housing Act is an important step forward. But as it moves through the legislative process, there is still an opportunity to broaden its ambition. A stronger focus on re-use, better implementation support, dedicated financing and a more people-centred approach would help turn a useful regulatory framework into a more comprehensive response to Europe’s housing affordability challenge.

Italy brought back border controls with Spain in August, and has now extended them until at least 15 October. Giorgia Meloni’s government fears that migrants who arrived in Ceuta, reach the continent and Italy.

Are these restrictions legal in the Schengen area? What are the EU’s levies to avoid such controls?

Since 1 August, Italy has temporarily reintroduced controls at its air and sea borders with Spain. The measure has now been extended until 15 October. In return, Spain has also introduced controls at its air and sea borders with Italy.

“This is not against Spain” the Italian foreign affairs minister Antonio Tajani said, adding “we have a duty to protect our borders.”

The starting point was the arrival of tens of thousands of migrants in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the end of July. Italy said it was concerned about possible secondary movements towards the rest of Europe, and brought back controls at its borders with Spain.

But from a legal point of view, EU countries can’t simply reintroduce border controls whenever they want.

The Schengen area is based on the principle of free movement, meaning there should normally be no checks at internal borders. The Schengen Borders Code provides an exception. If a country faces a serious threat to public policy or internal security, it can temporarily reintroduce border controls, as a measure of last resort.

The controls can initially be introduced for up to 30 days, and can then be extended under certain conditions.

Read more

THIS WEEK: Interior ministers discuss Fortress Europe, as Kallas goes to Syria

Italy has already extended its measure, which has now been in place for more than two months.

What does the European Commission say about Italy’s decision? The Commission has been asked about the Italian controls and says it is currently assessing the situation.

But the Brussels-based organisation The Good Lobby argues that Italy is violating the Schengen rules. It filed a complaint with the European Commission, asking it to open an infringement procedure against Italy.

According to Alberto Alemanno, who filed the complaint, there is no security threat that would justify bringing back the controls.

His argument is that none of the migrants who arrived in Ceuta were transferred to Italy. And, he says, people travelling between Ceuta and mainland Spain are already subject to identity checks.

So Italy’s justification, he argues, does not meet the conditions set out in the Schengen Borders Code.

Now, is Italy the only EU country bringing back border controls? No. If you look at the notifications sent by EU countries to the European Commission, around ten countries have reported temporary controls at some of their internal borders in recent months.

Read more

EU’s new cross‑border work rules favour recruitment, not workers, say critics

In response to the situation in Ceuta, Italy is the main example.

Austria also notified the Commission of controls in September, citing the situation in Ceuta among several reasons. But those controls concern its land borders with Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovenia.

So Austria is not checking passengers arriving by air from Spain.

Germany, for example, has invoked the same exception in the Schengen rules to carry out controls at its land borders with all its neighbours.

That does not mean that every border crossing is closed, or that every traveller is systematically checked. It means German authorities can carry out checks at those borders, including spot checks.

Germany’s main justification is continued migratory pressure, alongside other security concerns. And for now, the Commission is kind of letting all of this happen. It did raise concerns at some point: in June, the Commission published an assessment of temporary border controls in nine EU countries, including Germany, Austria and Italy.

It did not formally declare these countries’ controls illegal. Instead, it called on them to work towards lifting the controls, arguing that the EU has put in place measures to address some of the risks being invoked to justify them.

Those measures include the new Migration and Asylum Pact and new rules on entry and border management. The bigger question, then, is how long temporary border controls can remain in place before they stop being an exception to Schengen and become the new normal.

Donald Trump is betting on voluntary commitments from AI companies. On Tuesday (29 September), he unveiled a self-regulatory agreement drawn up with some of the biggest names in the AI industry.

What does it mean, and how does it differ from the EU’s Code of Practice for general-purpose AI?

On Tuesday, September 29, Trump brought together the CEOs of some of the biggest AI companies. Together, they signed what could be described as a self-regulation pact: a short list of non-binding commitments called the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.

Read more

AI chatbots turn users’ most intimate data into a potential goldmine for advertisers, researchers warn

That’s the other novelty: Trump no longer wants to talk about artificial intelligence, but about “super intelligence”. The term AI apparently has negative connotations.

So, what exactly have these companies committed to? The CEOs of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, SpaceX and Nvidia have pledged to put safeguards in place, quickly detect and fix problems, and have their systems checked by independent auditors.

The principle of voluntary commitments may sound familiar to Europeans: They echo the EU’s Code of Practice for general-purpose AI — which, like the White House agreement, is not legally binding.

So what’s the difference? First of all, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have also signed the EU code, while Meta, SpaceX and Nvidia have not.

And, more importantly, the EU does have binding rules in place: the AI Act, which is already in force. As part of this regulation, the European Commission developed the Code of Practice to help companies comply with the rules.

You could think of it as a checklist for AI companies, to help them make sure they are complying with the law.

Read more

Let’s not allow AI firms to use fears of future dystopias to distract Europeans from existing problems

Another difference is the sheer volume of recommendations. The document published by Trump is just one page long. The European Code of Practice runs to more than 60 pages and was prepared with the help of dozens of independent experts.

It is also more comprehensive, covering not only safety, but also transparency and copyright. But this raises another question: if both documents are voluntary,  how effective can they actually be?

When the European Code of Practice was published, some civil society organisations criticised it, arguing that voluntary commitments are not enough and that concrete obligations are needed.

Read more

EU states urged to ‘go beyond’ AI Act to protect people from abusive surveillance

There are binding obligations under the AI Act. But they are not as precise as what is in the code of conduct.

Similar criticisms have emerged since the White House agreement was published on Tuesday. And it is worse in the US case, since companies are absolutely not legally bound by the commitments they have made.

The United States has generally been less inclined towards binding regulation of the sector. Trump has argued that rules can hinder the development of companies, and has promoted a national framework that is as minimally restrictive as possible.

The White House document does leave the door open to legislation in the future. It says that, over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into lows or regulations.

But for now, they remain voluntary commitments. If you are interested in this topic, there will be a live event on Tuesday next week about AI and its safeguards, organised by VoxEurope.

 It will be online and you can find all information on Vox Europe website.

]]> Europe’s children will inherit public-health crisis from new EU pesticide approvals https://euobserver.com/240266/europes-children-will-inherit-public-health-crisis-from-new-eu-pesticide-approvals/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 09:37:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240266 By extending pesticide approvals and keeping hazardous products on the market, Brussels is bending to Big Pharma and causing a food-system and public-health burden for decades to come.]]> The European Union once prided itself on leading the world in protecting children. Today, policymakers backed by big polluters are betraying that promise in the name of “competitiveness”. 

In June 2026, Florence, Franck, and Isabelle packed their bags and headed to Brussels. Why? Because their children have all suffered serious harm from pesticides. 

These children have endured physical pain and heavy medical procedures, including repeated chemotherapy treatments. And their families have shouldered both the financial and emotional burdens alongside them.

As Isabelle puts it: “It destroys a family.” Her own daughter has been fighting leukaemia for the last seven years.

And they are not alone. In 2024, almost one in 20 children in the EU were exposed to dangerous levels of pesticides; that’s 380,000 kids. Now these parents have a clear message for policymakers: prioritise public health and stop dismantling the rules that protect children against harmful substances. 

In 2024, around 316,000 tonnes of toxic pesticides were sold in the EU to be sprayed across our countryside, risking not only the health of farmers but also polluting our soil, air and water.  

The European Environment Agency in Copenhagen has reported environmentally unsafe levels of pesticides in about a quarter of Europe’s rivers. In groundwater – which supplies 65 percent of the water we drink in Europe – unsafe levels were detected in 11-18 percent of water bodies. 

In the same year, trifluoroacetic acid, a harmful “forever chemical” that forms when ‘PFAS’ pesticides and F-gases break down, showed up in 94 percent of drinking water samples tested across 11 EU countries. 

We are surrounded by pesticide pollution. It’s even in our homes. 

But what’s happening in Brussels?

In December 2025, the European Commission proposed a legislative package that would remove fundamental environmental and health protections against pesticides in the EU.

Among other changes, the proposal – ironically labelled the ‘Food and Feed Safety’ Omnibus – suggests extending pesticide approvals indefinitely and relaxing the rules to allow pesticides already identified as hazardous to remain on the EU market. 

Let that sink in, no pun intended.

These proposals are a political choice to prioritise short-term profits for Big Polluters over children’s lives, people’s health, and the nature and ecosystems we need to survive.

Human health is at stake, and children are at particular risk – as they absorb substances more easily and are less able to excrete them. 

Pesticide exposure is linked to the development of childhood cancers, hormone disruption, neurodevelopmental impairments and birth defects. And prenatal and early childhood exposure can permanently alter development, with consequences that can be irreversible – and deadly.  

Under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, as well as the UN-declared human right to a healthy environment, all EU countries must commit to protecting children from environmental harm and ensure the highest attainable standard of health.

These principles must guide the work of EU institutions. 

Yet, instead of strengthening protections, the EU is moving backwards at a worrying speed. This is largely due to intense (and repeated) lobbying from multi-billion euro corporations, which includes the pesticides industry. Corporate chemical giants now spend €46m a year just to lobby the EU; that’s over 60 percent more than in 2020. 

Make it make sense

The incoherence of current EU policy is troubling. On the one hand, the EU Commission is celebrating its new Intergenerational Fairness Strategy – a framework that is meant to ensure today’s policies do not disadvantage future generations. On the other, the same institution is actively seeking to relax controls of harmful substances. 

Ripping up rules that protect people and the planet only benefits Big Polluters, industries that already make billions in profits at the expense of children’s health.

What’s more, an independent assessment found that the measures the EU institutions propose “will not accelerate innovations and authorisations”. In short, these proposals would actually make Europe less competitive.

Children’s rights and youth organisations have warned that deregulation exposes children to serious (and preventable) health risks. And the international scientific community recently stressed that robust environmental risk assessments cannot be optional.

Ultimately, Europe should widen and accelerate its access to pesticide-free alternatives. It must also support farmers in their efforts to transition away from pesticides, towards a more sustainable and resilient model.

So, what can be done? First, the EU must close the tap on pesticide use and production, and support farmers transitioning to safer alternatives. Second, it’s time for leaders to hold Big Polluters accountable for the damage they cause – not force the bill onto regular taxpayers and families harmed by these toxic substances.

Florence, Franck, and Isabelle’s children are among the hundreds of thousands already affected by pesticides. And they show that victims of pesticides are not just a statistic.

Employment agencies used fictitious student status to make foreign workers cheaper to employ, while private universities issued certificates that could help foreigners obtain visas or legalise their stay.

An investigation by the Polish publication Onet found the same schools and universities repeatedly appearing in documents issued to foreign workers from around the world. The schemes went beyond fake student cards. Private universities also issued certificates used to obtain visas, enter the Schengen area or legalise residency.

Fake students cheaper for employers

Polish labour laws incentivise employment of students aged up to 26 under so-called agreements to perform a job. It means employers do not have to pay social security or health insurance contributions for them. The workers cost less than regular employees.

So, student status has become a sought-after commodity that employment agencies have exploited for gains.

A central figure in the case is Dariusz M., a school head in Sieradz detained by police in late May. When reporters from TVN24 posed as employers looking for a way to legalise the employment of foreign immigrants, M. offered to enrol them as students for 750 zloty (around €175) per person.

Prosecutors suspect him of participating in an organised group that allegedly issued around 2,500 false study certificates, costing the Polish state nearly six million zloty (more than €1.4m) in unpaid contributions.

Documents were often arranged by employment agencies with foreign workers unaware they had formally been enrolled at a school.

“In most cases, they do not even know they are involved in something illegal. They trust the employment agency,” said Rocio Flores, president of the Union of Latin American Workers in Poland.

When an inspection uncovers the fraud, the foreign workers face losing their jobs, residency problems and, in some cases, deportation. “We migrants suffer most as a result,” Flores said.

Inspections carried out by Poland’s social insurance authority confirmed there were many such cases.

In August, Dziennik Gazeta Prawna reported that Poland’s social insurance body (ZUS) stepped up inspections of companies employing foreigners with pupil or student status.

They reported that inspectors uncovered cases in which agencies pay schools for fake study certificates despite the worker having never attended classes, with Poland’s social welfare system losing out on millions of zloty.

Schools oblivious to study scam

Not all paperwork for fake students came from education institutions themselves. Some student cards and study certificates were forged in the name of real schools without their knowledge, as was the case of a Cosinus network branch in the town of Piaseczno.

Its head, Elżbieta Gotchold-Leśniewski, showed Onet reporters a file containing 62 forgeries found in various parts of Poland and had been issued to people from South America, Africa, Asia and Europe. “That is not my signature, and the school’s hologram is wrong too. ]]> AI chatbots turn users’ most intimate data into a potential goldmine for advertisers, researchers warn https://euobserver.com/239963/ai-chatbots-turn-users-most-intimate-data-into-a-potential-goldmine-for-advertisers-researchers-warn/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 06:51:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=239963 Researchers found that even when users rejected non-essential cookies, Perplexity, DeepSeek, Gemini, Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude still connected to Google Ads.]]> Six out of nine of the most popular AI chatbots routinely exposed user input to third parties, new European research reveals.

Multiple chatbots disclosed sensitive user data to advertising companies through trackers – a piece of code used to identify and target users on the web with customised advertisements, which are widely used across the web.

And tech companies may have been able to link conversation summaries with personal identifiers, allowing users to be targeted based on their conversations with AI.

The researchers aimed to establish the connection between existing tracking technologies and AI advertising. “We basically connected the dots, and wanted to test whether and how AI bots integrate tracking and advertising services,” said Narseo Vallina-Rodriguez, who led the study.

Vallina-Rodriguez is part of a group of researchers who investigated the use of ad trackers in the most popular AI providers with colleagues at Imdea Networks, a public research institute in Madrid.

Their findings warn of “tensions” between tech company practices and obligations to users under privacy laws.

Sensitive user-data shared 

“We already knew that tracking is pervasive, even without AI. But now you have the most super-invasive phenomena on the internet, which is AI,” said Itxaso Domínguez de Olazábal, a policy adviser at digital rights group Edri.

Users often share information about their health, psychological state, finances, and other intimate matters in AI prompts. The study shows how users who asked AI questions about such matters could have sensitive details summarised in a chat title shared with third parties. 

“Now, big tech has access to much more intimate information which users tell AI. It’s crazy, the details are so intimate. My friends ask AI bots about relationships, or they use ‘doctor AI’,” said Domínguez de Olazábal.

GDPR rules require companies to make clear how users’ data is harvested, but researchers question “ambiguous expressions” used to explain the role of trackers in T&Cs.

And the ePrivacy directive requires users to consent to cookies unless they are “strictly necessary”, but researchers found that even when users rejected non-essential cookies, AI bots Perplexity, DeepSeek, Gemini, Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude still connected to Google Ads.

All of the top nine most popular chatbots were found to integrate at least one third-party advertising or tracking service.

Consent and transparency ‘shortcomings’

A preview of the study, released in May, prompted the Spanish privacy watchdog AEPD to request for the European Data Protection Committee (EPDC) to share preliminary findings with European counterparts “for knowledge and assessment”.

The final paper, titled ‘Prompt like a Butterfly, Sting like a Tracker’, has been accepted for publication at an academic forum in Delft next year.

Findings “highlight tensions between current practices and obligations under the GDPR and ePrivacy Directive, exposing broader shortcomings in consent, access control, and transparency mechanisms,” the paper reads.

It reveals that Grok, operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI, exposed public links to conversations by default, allowing trackers to routinely access whole conversations, with TikTok also processing screenshots of Grok conversations.

    • The Ukrainian army stays in control of front lines, but safety in cities deteriorates. The war has reached a stage in which two separate conflicts appear to be taking place simultaneously.

    While Ukraine is currently losing the battle in the air and its cities are continually suffering missile and strikes by jet drones, the situation on battlefields is far better.

    Last week, Denník N spent time in Ukraine with former chief of the general staff Daniel Zmeko. During the trip, reporters met commanding officers from several brigades and battalions operating from the Izium area to Zaporizhzhia, and all of them said they had the situation under control.

    The officers spoke about the accuracy of Russian maps, which they said did not correspond to reality. In some places, Russian soldiers are as far as 20 km from the locations where, according to the Kremlin, they are supposed to be.

    Northern flank of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration: This is a specific section of the front where the Ukrainian army has been reporting its advances only very slowly, while Ukrainian analysts have remained silent so as not to disclose anything sensitive. Russian bloggers, by contrast, are depicting the situation more closely to reality.

    Yet official Russian maps persist with utterly nonsensical lines. We do not know to what extent this is an effort to deceive domestic and foreign audiences, and to what extent they genuinely believe it in Moscow. It is worth looking at how the regime wants the situation to appear, and what it is really like.

    The first map in the overview was produced by the Russian state news agency RIA Novosti and depicts the area around Lyman, on the northern flank of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk direction, as of 29 September. Lyman is shown as occupied in the middle of the map. The map’s author also continues to insist that the Russian army had captured Sviatohirsk — at the tip of the red salient in the centre of the map — and that Russia controls the entire, now non-existent salient with the village of Novoselivka at its centre.     The following map is much closer to reality. According to it, the front line roughly follows the Zherebets river, which corresponds to Rybar’s claims.

    Rybar’s map looks like this:

    Kupiansk direction: The city of Kupiansk is a similar case to Sviatohirsk. Putin declared it captured in August last year.     For example, the Kremlin agency claims that the Ukrainian bridgehead on the eastern bank of the Oskil river south of the city no longer exists. Ukrainians do face major difficulties supplying it, and various analysts have repeatedly warned of an impending disaster, but the Russian map is nevertheless hopelessly inaccurate.

    Also note the small town of Borova at the bottom centre. RIA Novosti also shows it as occupied, although this is not the case.

Borova is again at the bottom centre, while below Kupiansk is the Ukrainian bridgehead that Russia claims does not exist.

    Orikhiv: This is one of the places where Ukrainian officers said during reporters’ trip to Ukraine that Russian maps were particularly inaccurate.
